notable_claims: University of Hawaii's computer policy asserts that computer use is a privilege, not a right.
Wayne State University and Ohio State University allegedly bypassed student due process policies by claiming denial of computer access was not 'disciplinary action'.
The Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) of 1986 provides exemptions for service providers to access electronic communications.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes several incidents regarding academic computing rights, including disputes over intellectual property theft and the denial of due process for students losing computer access at Wayne State University and Ohio State University. It critiques a University of Hawaii policy that treats computer use as a privilege rather than a right, allowing administrative searches without notice. Additionally, it discusses email privacy laws (ECPA 1986) in the context of an MCI Mail snooping incident.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.45

notable_claims: An influential professional is attempting to pass off a project as belonging to a powerful organization
Original attributions and descriptions were deleted during the adaptation of a disk copy for printing
classification.summary: Diane Kovacs seeks advice regarding a situation where an influential professional is allegedly misappropriating her project. She claims the individual is attempting to attribute the work to a powerful organization after removing original attributions and descriptions during a printing process. Kovacs expresses concern that challenging this theft could jeopardize her early career.
classification.title: Intellectual Property Theft...Help

notable_claims: Documentation is the most powerful weapon in intellectual property disputes.
Academic institutions are generally sensitive to intellectual property issues.
classification.summary: Leo Geoffrion responds to a plea for help from Diane Kovacs regarding the alleged theft of her project by an influential professional. Geoffrion advises on strategies for fighting intellectual property disputes within academic institutions, emphasizing meticulous documentation and identifying appropriate administrative complaint channels.
classification.title: Re: Intellectual Property Theft...Help.

notable_claims: Computer policies that allow summary suspension before establishing guilt violate due process and academic freedom.
Discretionary searches of user email and files by system administrators may violate the 4th Amendment.
The term 'frivolous' in computer use policies is too vague to be enforceable without infringing on free expression.
Academic freedom principles require that the user community participate in the creation and enforcement of computer policies.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides a critique of the computer policy at the University of Hawaii's College of Engineering. He argues that the policy violates due process by allowing summary suspensions and infringes on privacy by permitting discretionary searches of email and files without notice. The post emphasizes that academic freedom requires user participation in policy creation and protection against vague prohibitions, such as those against 'frivolous' messages.
classification.title: Article 3--Re: policy

notable_claims: WSU C&IT claimed that denying computer access to 'protect other users' is not a disciplinary action and thus exempt from the Student Due Process Policy.
classification.summary: John Palmer shares a 1991 letter from Wayne State University (WSU) regarding the denial of computing access to a student. The university argued that denying computer access based on past abuse was not a 'disciplinary action' and therefore did not trigger the Student Due Process Policy.
classification.title: Wayne State University's Bad Behavior Continues Unabated....

identity.subject: Article 4--Wayne State University's Bad Behavior Continues Unabated....

notable_claims: Universities may redefine 'discipline' to avoid providing due process when revoking computer access.
The case of Steven Brack at Ohio State involved a dismissal from the computer system without proper disciplinary procedure.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the denial of due process for students losing computer access at Wayne State and Ohio State Universities. He argues that universities use semantic redefinitions to claim that removing computer privileges is not 'discipline' and therefore does not require due process. The post provides a list of legal references and case files regarding Steven Brack's dismissal from Ohio State University systems.
classification.title: Re: Wayne State University's Bad Behavior Continues Unabated....

notable_claims: The previous SFA policy required permission for all postings, which was challenged as a First Amendment violation.
The settlement established that the school could only remove signs if they were deemed to incite 'imminent lawlessness'.
classification.summary: A news report detailing a settlement between Stephen F. Austin University and the Young Conservatives of Texas over a dispute regarding campus posting policies. The conflict began when students posted fliers containing a quote from Barry Goldwater, which school officials deemed sexist. The resulting settlement led to a new policy allowing posters while maintaining 'time, place and manner' restrictions.
classification.title: [UPI] SFA free speech flap settled

notable_claims: Computing resources are intended for educational purposes and legitimate university business.
Commercial use or financial gain using university computing resources is prohibited.
Reverse-assembling or reverse-compiling licensed software is restricted.
Electronic communications must meet the same standards as tangible documents regarding forgery and attribution.
organizations: Office of Computing and Information Technology (CIT)
classification.summary: This item shares the official computing and network resource guidelines issued by Princeton University for the 1992-1993 academic year. The policy outlines acceptable use, prohibits commercial gain, and integrates university codes of conduct regarding harassment and intellectual property. It specifically addresses technical behaviors such as password security, unauthorized access, and the prohibition of reverse-compiling licensed software.
classification.title: New Princeton Policy: 1992-1993 Guidelines for use of Campus and Network Computing Resources

notable_claims: MCI Mail allegedly saved messages for five days before deletion in 1992.
Evidence from MCI Mail accounts led to civil suits and search warrants regarding the theft of confidential marketing plans.
classification.summary: The post discusses email privacy and the legal implications of 'snooping' in corporate environments. It references a San Francisco Examiner report regarding civil suits against Symantec and Borland executives based on evidence found in MCI Mail accounts. The author questions the ethics and legality of system administrators reading user emails during account closure.
classification.title: Article 8--Re: Article on E-mail Privacy/Snooping

notable_claims: The Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986 (Section 2701(c)(1)) exempts service providers from prohibitions against accessing stored communications.
Service providers may divulge contents of a communication to law enforcement if they were inadvertently obtained and appear to pertain to a crime (Section 2702(b)(6)).
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the legality of a system administrator reading a user's email during account deletion. Joseph A. Watters argues that under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986, service providers are exempt from certain prohibitions against accessing stored communications and may disclose inadvertently discovered evidence of crimes to law enforcement.
classification.title: Article 9--Re: Article on E-mail Privacy/Snooping

notable_claims: Some LAN administrators manually screened user directories for 'personal' content during account deletion in the absence of formal company policy.
The debate highlights a tension between the right to privacy and the administrative need to preserve business-critical data after an employee departs.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the ethics and legality of system administrators accessing user emails and files during account closure. The thread contrasts a legal case involving MCI Mail with common industry practices where admins manually screened files to distinguish personal data from company assets.
classification.title: Article 10--Re: Article on E-mail Privacy/Snooping

notable_claims: The volume of data on a LAN does not preclude targeted snooping of specific individuals.
classification.summary: Mike O'Connor responds to a claim that the sheer volume of files on a Local Area Network (LAN) prevents effective snooping. He argues that targeted surveillance is still feasible if an administrator focuses on specific individuals with organized directories.
classification.title: Article 11--Re: Article on E-mail Privacy/Snooping

notable_claims: The ECPA of 1986 allows service provider employees to intercept communications if it is a 'necessary incident' to the rendition of service.
There is ambiguity regarding whether reading messages before account deletion constitutes a necessary duty or illegal snooping.
Electronic communications may not have the same evidentiary prohibitions as wire or oral communications under certain sections of Title 18.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the legality of an MCI Mail employee reading a user's emails before closing an account. The participants analyze whether such actions are protected under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) of 1986, specifically focusing on 'necessary incident' exceptions for service providers.
classification.title: Article 12--Re: MCI E-mail Snooping
